entry: American mathematician, electrical engineer and cryptographer, known as the father of information theory. His master's thesis (1937) showed that [[Boolean algebra]] could be applied to electrical circuits to construct any logical numerical relationship, establishing the theory behind digital computing and digital circuits. During World War II he contributed to cryptanalysis for United States national defense, and a paper he wrote is considered one of the foundational pieces of [[Cryptography|modern cryptography]]. His 1948 paper "A Mathematical Theory of Communication" laid the foundations of [[Information theory]]; he formally introduced the term "bit." He joined the [[Central Intelligence Agency]]'s advisory group in 1951 and was a professor at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|MIT]] from 1956 to 1978. He co-organized the 1956 Dartmouth workshop, considered the founding event of [[Artificial intelligence|artificial intelligence]].

Italian composer, choirmaster and string player, a transitional figure between the Renaissance and [[Baroque music|Baroque]] periods. He worked at the court of Mantua (c. 1590–1613) before becoming maestro di cappella at the basilica of San Marco in the [[Republic of Venice]]. A pioneer of opera, he wrote three surviving complete operas; *L'Orfeo* (1607) is the earliest opera still widely performed. His surviving music also includes nine books of madrigals and sacred works such as the *Vespro della Beata Vergine* (1610). He worked in the Renaissance polyphonic tradition but also employed the basso continuo, a technique distinctive of the Baroque. His works were largely forgotten in the 18th and much of the 19th centuries and were rediscovered at the beginning of the 20th century.

Roman emperor (r. AD 41–54), fourth ruler of the [[Julio-Claudian dynasty]] and the first Roman emperor born outside Italy. Declared emperor by the Praetorian Guard after the assassination of [[Caligula]], he was an able administrator who expanded the imperial bureaucracy to include freedmen. He built roads, aqueducts and canals, and the Empire began its conquest of Britain during his reign. Many authors contend that he was murdered by his wife, Agrippina the Younger.

Grammatical unit consisting of a subject and a predicate, typically built around a verb. A complete simple [[Sentence (linguistics)|sentence]] contains a single clause with a finite verb. An independent clause can stand alone as a sentence, while a dependent clause relies on an independent clause; dependent clauses often begin with subordinating conjunctions such as *because*, *although* or *if*. Finite clauses contain a verb marked for tense, person and number, whereas non-finite clauses use infinitives, gerunds or participles and lack independent tense. Standard subject-verb clauses are the norm in English and are usually declarative. The subject may be unexpressed when it is deducible from context, as in English imperatives.

[[Bone|Long bone]] forming a strut between the shoulder blade and the sternum, also called the collarbone. The clavicle is a slender, S-shaped bone about 15 cm (6 in) long, with one on each side of the body. It is the only long bone that lies horizontally, and together with the shoulder blade it forms the shoulder girdle. Its name comes from [[Latin]] *clavicula*, "little key," because the bone rotates like a key when the shoulder is raised. It is the most commonly broken bone, often fractured by a fall onto an outstretched [[Arm|arm]].

Fine-grained natural soil composed of clay minerals, hydrous aluminum phyllosilicates such as kaolinite. Most pure clay minerals are white, and natural clays take on colors from impurities such as iron oxide. Clay develops plasticity when wet and hardens when fired, making it the longest-known [[Ceramic|ceramic]] raw material. Prehistoric people used it for [[Pottery]]; some of the earliest pottery shards have been dated to around 14,000 BCE, and clay tablets were the first known writing medium. Clay is used in [[Paper]] making, [[Cement]] production and chemical filtering. Between one-half and two-thirds of the world's population live or work in buildings made with clay. Shale, formed largely from clay, is the most common [[Sedimentary rock|sedimentary rock]]. Expansive clays, which swell when they absorb water, are a major challenge in [[Civil engineering]].

British statesman, Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 1945 to 1951 and leader of the [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour Party]] from 1935 to 1955. He was deputy prime minister in the wartime coalition led by [[Winston Churchill]] from 1942. Labour's landslide victory in the 1945 general election brought him to power. His government nationalized major industries, created the National Health Service in 1948 and expanded state welfare, including the National Insurance Act 1946. Its foreign policy oversaw [[Decolonization|decolonization]], including the [[Partition of India|partition of India]] in 1947. Attlee backed the Marshall Plan and the [[NATO]] alliance, and sent British troops to fight in the [[Korean War]]. Labour narrowly lost the 1951 general election despite winning the most votes.

Christian theologian and philosopher who taught at the Catechetical School of [[Alexandria]]. Among his pupils were [[Origen]] and Alexander of Jerusalem. A convert to Christianity, he was familiar with classical Greek philosophy and literature. His three major works show Hellenistic influence to a greater extent than any other Christian thinker of his time, particularly that of [[Plato]] and the Stoics. In one work he argued that Greek philosophy originated among non-Greeks, claiming that Plato and [[Pythagoras]] were taught by Egyptian scholars. He is usually regarded as a Church Father and is venerated as a saint in Coptic Christianity, Eastern Catholicism, Ethiopian Christianity and Anglicanism. His name was removed from the Roman Martyrology in 1586.

Bishop of Rome (c. 88–99) and one of the Apostolic Fathers of the Church. Tertullian claimed that [[Saint Peter]] ordained him, though early church lists differ on his place among the bishops of Rome. His only known genuine surviving writing is *1 Clement*, a letter to the church at Corinth that asserted the authority of presbyters appointed by the apostles. The letter is one of the oldest extant Christian documents outside the [[New Testament]] and is considered the earliest affirmation of the principle of apostolic succession. He is likely to have died in exile around 100, possibly as a martyr. He is recognized as a saint in many Christian churches and is a patron saint of mariners.

Formal leaders within established religions. Their roles vary by tradition but usually involve presiding over rituals and teaching doctrine and practice. In [[Christianity]], titles vary by denomination and include [[Priest|priests]], bishops, deacons, elders, pastors and [[Pope|popes]]. In [[Islam]], a religious leader is often called an [[Imam|imam]], caliph, mufti or mullah. In [[Judaism]], a leader is often a [[Rabbi|rabbi]] (teacher) or hazzan (cantor). Women's inclusion in the clergy grew from the 19th century, and in 2016 they made up about 20.7% of U.S. clergy.

City (pop., 2020: 372,624) in northeastern [[Ohio]], on the southern shore of [[Lake Erie]] and county seat of Cuyahoga County. Founded in 1796 near the mouth of the Cuyahoga River, it was named after General Moses Cleaveland and became a major commercial and industrial city by the late 19th century. It was among the top 10 largest U.S. cities by population for much of the 20th century. From the 1960s its economy slowed as manufacturing declined and suburbanization occurred. The city is a port connected to the Atlantic Ocean via the [[St. Lawrence Seaway]]. Its economy now relies on higher education, healthcare and financial services. Cultural institutions include the Cleveland Museum of Art, the Cleveland Orchestra and the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]].

Steep, nearly vertical rock face. Cliffs form through [[Weathering|weathering]] and [[Erosion|erosion]], with the effect of gravity, and are common on coasts, in mountainous areas and along rivers. They are usually composed of resistant rock, such as [[Sandstone]], limestone, [[Chalk]] and dolomite, while igneous rocks such as [[Granite]] and [[Basalt]] also often form cliffs. An escarpment is a cliff formed by movement along a [[Fault (geology)|fault]], by landslides or by differential erosion of rock layers. Most cliffs have a scree slope at their base. Coastal erosion may create sea cliffs along a receding coastline.

British singer and actor, dominant in British popular music in the late 1950s and early 1960s with his backing group, the Shadows. His 1958 single "Move It" is often described as Britain's first authentic rock and roll song. He represented the United Kingdom in the [[Eurovision Song Contest]] in 1968 and 1973. He has achieved 14 UK No. 1 singles and, by the late 1990s, had sold more than 250 million records worldwide.

American anthropologist and leading figure of symbolic and interpretive anthropology. After a PhD from [[Harvard University]] in 1956, he conducted fieldwork in [[Java]], [[Bali]] and [[Morocco]], analyzing religion, economy and social structure through symbols. His 1973 essay collection *The Interpretation of Cultures* argued that anthropological insight comes from "thick description" that interprets the meanings people attach to their actions. Critics argued that this approach sacrificed empirical testability and universality. For three decades he was considered "the single most influential cultural anthropologist in the United States." He ended his career as professor emeritus at the Institute for Advanced Study, Princeton.

Variations in climate that persist longer than individual weather events, from seasons to millennia. [[Climate change|Climate change]] refers to variations persisting for decades or more and is now often used for contemporary global warming. The climate system receives nearly all its energy from the [[Sun|sun]]; when incoming energy exceeds outgoing energy, the climate warms. Internal variability arises from natural processes, such as the Pacific decadal oscillation and Atlantic multidecadal oscillation, while external forcing includes changes in solar output and volcanism. Since the [[Industrial Revolution]], human activities have increasingly affected the climate, and atmospheric CO₂ has risen from about 280 ppm to over 420 ppm. Some analyses emphasize human dominance in recent warming, while others highlight natural variability.

Scientific study of Earth's climate, regarded as part of the [[Atmospheric science|atmospheric sciences]] and a subdivision of [[Physical geography]]. Climate is often defined as the distribution of weather conditions over a period of at least 30 years. Climatology's main research topics are climate variability, the mechanisms of climate change and modern climate change. Its methods include analysis of observations and modeling of the physical processes that determine climate. Climatologists study cycles such as the [[El Niño–Southern Oscillation]] (ENSO), the North Atlantic oscillation (NAO) and the Pacific decadal oscillation (PDO), which also inform short-term [[Weather forecasting|weather forecasting]]. Climatology includes some aspects of [[Oceanography]] and biogeochemistry.

Activity of ascending steep objects using the hands, feet and other parts of the body, from the world's tallest mountains to small boulders. Climbing is done for locomotion, sport and competition, and in trades such as construction and military operations. It takes place indoors on artificial walls and outdoors on natural surfaces, in disciplines including [[Rock climbing|rock climbing]] and ice climbing. Other disciplines include bouldering and sport climbing, while [[Mountaineering]] combines climbing with hiking and navigation to reach high summits. Climbing made its Olympic debut at Tokyo 2020, with combined events in bouldering, lead and speed on artificial walls.

Branch of psychology concerned with the research, assessment, diagnosis and treatment of emotional and behavioral disorders, and with promoting well-being. Its central practices are psychological assessment, diagnosis, clinical formulation and [[Psychotherapy|psychotherapy]]. The field is generally considered to have begun in 1896, when Lightner Witmer opened the first psychological clinic at the [[University of Pennsylvania]]. Assessment dominated until World War II created a need for many more trained clinicians. Unlike [[Psychiatry|psychiatrists]], who are medical doctors, clinical psychologists treat [[Mental disorder|mental disorders]] mainly through psychotherapy. In nine US states, clinical psychologists with advanced specialty training may prescribe psychotropic medications.

American actor and filmmaker known for Westerns and action films. He rose to fame as the "Man with No Name" in Sergio Leone's Dollars Trilogy of spaghetti Westerns in the mid-1960s, and as police inspector Harry Callahan in the *Dirty Harry* films of the 1970s and 1980s. He directed many films, including the Western *Unforgiven* (1992) and the sports drama *Million Dollar Baby* (2004); both won the [[Academy Awards|Academy Awards]] for Best Picture and Best Director. His company Malpaso Productions has produced all but four of his American films since 1967. He served as mayor of Carmel-by-the-Sea, California, from 1986 to 1988.

Erectile female sex organ found in amniotes. In humans it is the most erogenous area of the vulva and generally the primary anatomical source of female sexual pleasure. The visible glans is roughly the size and shape of a pea and is estimated to have more than 10,000 nerve endings. The clitoris is homologous to most of the [[Penis]] in males, and its only known purpose is to provide sexual pleasure. Much of its structure is internal, with paired crura intertwined with the [[Urethra]] and [[Vagina]]. Knowledge of its anatomy is scant compared with that of male sex organs, and cultural perceptions contribute to stigmas. Debate has also centered on [[Female genital mutilation|female genital mutilation]] and the physiological basis of the [[G-spot]].

British writer, filmmaker and visual artist who came to prominence in the 1980s with the short-story series *Books of Blood*. He wrote and directed the first *Hellraiser* film (1987), based on his novella *The Hellbound Heart*. His work has also been adapted into the *Candyman* series. His paintings and illustrations have been shown in galleries in the United States, and he has created characters and series for comic books.

Posterior opening that serves as the only outlet for the digestive, reproductive and urinary tracts of many vertebrates. [[Amphibian|Amphibians]], [[Reptile|reptiles]], [[Bird|birds]], cartilaginous fish and a few [[Mammal|mammals]], including [[Monotreme|monotremes]], have one. Most placental mammals have separate openings for evacuation and reproduction. A cloacal gland in the region has been implicated in scent-marking in some reptiles, marsupials, amphibians and monotremes. Mating through the cloaca is called cloacal copulation.

Loose outer garment, almost always sleeveless, that fastens at the neck or over the shoulder. Cloaks protect the wearer from the weather in the manner of an overcoat and may form part of a [[Uniform|uniform]]. They vary in length from hip to ankle, with mid-calf the normal length, and may have an attached hood. Designs have changed over time to match fashion and the available [[Textile|textiles]]. In [[Ancient Greece|ancient Greece]], the himation was a rectangular woolen cloak wrapped around the body and draped over one shoulder. Christian clerics may wear a cappa or cope as liturgical vestments.

[[Benzodiazepine|Benzodiazepine]] medication used to prevent and treat anxiety disorders, seizures and akathisia. Sold under the brand name Klonopin, it is usually taken by mouth; effects begin within one hour and last eight to 12 hours in adults. It binds to GABAA receptors, increasing the effect of the inhibitory [[Neurotransmitter|neurotransmitter]] GABA. Long-term use can cause dependence and addiction, and withdrawal can be life-threatening. Patented in 1960 and approved in 1975 in the United States, it was the 62nd most commonly prescribed medication there in 2023.

Process of producing organisms or biological material with identical genomes, by natural or artificial means. In nature, some organisms clone themselves through [[Asexual reproduction|asexual reproduction]], including [[Parthenogenesis]]. In biotechnology, cloning produces copies of cells and DNA fragments. Artificial reproductive cloning is often accomplished by somatic-cell nuclear transfer (SCNT), which creates an [[Embryo|embryo]] from a somatic cell and an [[Egg cell|egg cell]]. In 1996, [[Dolly (sheep)|Dolly]] the sheep became the first mammal cloned from an adult somatic cell. Cloning has been proposed as a means of reviving extinct species, and the use of embryonic [[Stem cell|stem cells]] in some research has attracted controversy. Human cloning is a subject of ethical debate and a frequent theme in science fiction.
